title: flag and subcommands, environment variables, stdin
summary: A FlagSet per command parses an explicit argument slice and returns errors instead of exiting; environment variables feed flag defaults, so flags win. stdin is just an io.Reader.

examples.title: The flag syntax rules, run against a FlagSet

annotations.note: flag.Parse() parses os.Args into package-level globals and, on error, exits with code 2. A FlagSet with ContinueOnError returns the error instead, so the same function serves main and a table-driven test.
XxxVar binds a flag to a struct field. The default and the help text are part of the definition, and flag builds the usage message from them: look at the stderr pane.
One dash or two are the same flag, and -name=value and -name value both work. Typed flags parse on the spot: 1.5s becomes a time.Duration, and "many" is rejected as an int.
Parsing stops at the first non-flag argument, so -v after a.txt is a file name. GNU getopt and Python's argparse accept flags after positionals; Go does not.
A boolean flag is switched off only with -v=false: in "-v false" the false would be a positional argument. "--" ends the flags, so a file name that starts with a dash survives.

With ContinueOnError, flag has already printed the error and the usage to fs.Output() (stderr by default); the caller only picks the exit code. -h and -help return flag.ErrHelp, which by convention exits 0.

examples.title: Subcommands, and an environment variable as the flag's default

annotations.note: A map from subcommand name to function is all the dispatch a small tool needs. strings.ToUpperSpecial with a nil SpecialCase has no overrides, so it is plain Unicode casing; unicode.TurkishCase maps i to İ and ı to I.
Start from the built-in default and replace it with the environment value if there is one. An empty variable counts as unset here.

One FlagSet per subcommand, named after it, so subcommands can define different flags. The value so far becomes the flag's default: an explicit -lang overwrites the environment, and -h shows the effective default. SetOutput sends flag's messages to the injected stderr.
flag checks syntax, not meaning: "de" is a valid string. Validate after parsing and treat a bad value as a usage error, code 2.
A map-backed getenv lets tests run without touching the process environment, which is global: testing's t.Setenv refuses to run in parallel tests for exactly that reason.
os.LookupEnv has exactly the parameter's type. os.Setenv changes this process and the children it starts later, never the shell that started it.

examples.title: A tiny wc: stdin is an io.Reader
examples.stdin:
Merhaba dünya
İstanbul'da yağmur var
çay mı, kahve mi?

annotations.note: count never mentions os.Stdin. main passes stdin, a test passes strings.NewReader, and a file argument would pass an *os.File: the same accept-a-Reader shape as in the reading-files lesson.
ScanLines strips "\n" and a "\r" before it, so CRLF input from Windows tools counts the same as LF input from Unix ones.
chars matches wc -m and bytes matches wc -c, minus the newlines. They differ by 5 here because ü, İ, ğ, ç and ı take two bytes each in UTF-8.

os.Stdin is an ordinary *os.File. Run without a pipe, the program waits for the user to type and end the input, which looks like a hang; tools that default to stdin usually say so in their usage text.

use_cases: Internal tools and one-off migrations where a dependency for argument parsing isn't worth it
git-style tools with subcommands (tool import, tool export), each with its own flags
Twelve-factor services: configuration from environment variables, overridable by flags during development
Unix filters that read stdin and write stdout, so they compose with grep, sort and jq
strengths: No dependency for small tools: flag, os and bufio are in the standard library, while the JDK has no argument parser at all
Typed flags (Int, Duration, Bool) parse and validate in one step: -timeout 1.5s arrives as a time.Duration, not a string to parse later
Usage text is generated from the definitions, so -h can't drift from the code
With a FlagSet, an injected getenv and an io.Reader, the whole CLI runs in-process in a test, with no subprocess
weaknesses: No GNU conventions: -v and --v are the same flag, there are no short/long aliases (-v/--verbose) and no combined short flags (-xvf)
Flags must come before positional arguments; users used to GNU tools put them last and get them treated as file names
No required flags, no subcommand tree, no config-file binding: you write the checks, or reach for a third-party package once the CLI grows

pitfalls.title: Flags after positional arguments
pitfalls.detail: tool report.txt -v leaves -v in fs.Args(). Document flags-first usage, or check Args() for leftovers that start with a dash.

pitfalls.title: Turning a boolean off with a separate word
pitfalls.detail: -dry-run false sets dry-run to true and adds "false" as a positional argument.

pitfalls.title: os.Getenv can't tell unset from empty
pitfalls.detail: Both return "". Use os.LookupEnv when an empty value means something different from a missing one.

pitfalls.title: flag.Parse in init() or in a library
pitfalls.detail: Since Go 1.13 test flags are registered when the test binary starts, so a package that parses flags during initialization can break go test. Parse once, in main or run, and keep flag definitions out of libraries.

pitfalls.title: Turkish text piped from Windows PowerShell 5.1
pitfalls.detail: Text piped into a native program is encoded with $OutputEncoding, which defaults to US-ASCII there: İ and ı arrive as '?'. Set $OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new() first.

quiz.q: fs defines a bool flag -v. What does fs.Parse([]string{"report.txt", "-v"}) leave you with?
options: An error: flags must come first
quiz.why: Parsing stops at the first non-flag argument without error; everything after it, -v included, is positional.

quiz.q: A bool flag defaults to true. How does the user switch it off?
quiz.why: Boolean flags take a value only in the -flag=value form; in -color false, false is a positional argument.

quiz.q: The casing tool has -lang and reads CASING_LANG. Which order of precedence does it implement?
quiz.why: The environment value becomes the flag's default, and an explicit flag overwrites the default.

quiz.q: Why does run take getenv func(string) (string, bool) instead of calling os.Getenv?
options: Tests can pass a map without changing the process-wide environment
quiz.why: The environment is global to the process; os.Setenv in one test leaks into others and blocks t.Parallel. Injection keeps tests independent.

body:
## Concept

A command-line program has three inputs: its arguments, its environment and its
standard input. The `flag` package turns arguments into typed values; a `FlagSet`
does it for an explicit slice, which is how you build subcommands and how you test.
`os.LookupEnv` reads the environment and tells "unset" from "empty". `os.Stdin` is an
`*os.File`, so everything that reads an `io.Reader` reads stdin.

The common shape is precedence: a built-in default, overridden by an environment
variable, overridden by a flag. With `flag` that takes three lines, because the
environment value simply becomes the flag's default.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: GNU `getopt` permutes arguments and supports `-xvf`; `flag` does neither and
  stops at the first positional argument. `getenv` returning `NULL` for unset is what
  `os.LookupEnv`'s boolean gives you.
- Python: `argparse` is the closer match (stdlib, generated help, subparsers), but it
  accepts options after positionals. `os.environ.get` ≈ `os.LookupEnv`.
- Java: there is no argument parser in the JDK; `flag` plays the role of picocli or
  commons-cli for small tools. `System.getenv` returns `null` for unset, like
  LookupEnv's `false`.
- Node: `process.argv.slice(2)` ≈ `os.Args[1:]`, `process.env` ≈ the environment,
  `process.stdin` ≈ `os.Stdin`, but in Go reading it is plain blocking code.

## Design notes

Keep `main` as the only place that touches the process: `os.Exit(run(os.Args[1:],
os.LookupEnv, os.Stdin, os.Stdout, os.Stderr))`. Everything else takes its inputs as
parameters, so a table-driven test calls `run` with a slice, a map-backed `getenv` and a
`strings.Reader`, in parallel, with no subprocess.

Stay with `flag` while the tool is small. Since Go 1.16, `fs.Func` handles a repeatable
flag (`-H a -H b`) without writing a `flag.Value` type. When you need GNU-style
`--long`/`-s` pairs, nested subcommands, shell completion or config-file binding,
that is the point to adopt a CLI library, not before. For anything you pipe in from
Windows, remember the shell decides the encoding: make it UTF-8 and the Go side needs
nothing special.
